lessons.title: Reading notes on the treble stave

objectives: The notes on the treble lines — E, G, B, D, F
The notes in the treble spaces — F, A, C, E
How the treble clef fixes G on the second line
The three notes just outside the stave — middle C on its ledger line, D below the stave, G above it

concept.title: Reading the treble stave
concept.body: The treble clef curls around the second line up, which fixes that line as G — everything else is counted from there. The five **lines**, bottom to top, spell E, G, B, D, F: Every Good Boy Deserves Football. The four **spaces**, bottom to top, spell F, A, C, E, which is just the word face. Notes step through the alphabet as they climb, line, space, line, space, and after G it starts again at A. To name a note you do not recognise, find the nearest landmark you do know and count up or down from it one step at a time. Three more notes sit just outside the five lines. D hangs in the space below the bottom line, and G sits in the space above the top line. Middle C is lower still, and it needs a short ledger line of its own — the only ledger line Grade 1 asks for.

teach.smartTip: The four spaces spell the word FACE from the bottom up — the quickest notes to recall.
teach.didYouKnow: The treble clef is a stylised letter G — its curl loops right around the G line.

objectives: How many crotchet beats each note lasts
What the two numbers of a time signature mean
How note values add up to fill one bar, between two bar-lines
How a dot adds half a note's value again

concept.title: How long each note lasts
concept.body:
Music is divided into bars by thin vertical lines called bar-lines, and each bar holds the same amount of time. The time signature at the start says how much. Read it as two separate numbers, not as a fraction: the top number is how many beats are in each bar, and the bottom number says which note value gets one beat. A 4 on the bottom means the crotchet, so 3/4 is three crotchet beats in every bar. A double bar-line marks the end of a section, and a thin line followed by a thick one marks the end of the piece.

Each note value lasts twice as long as the next one down, so the whole family halves step by step: a semibreve is four crotchet beats, a minim two, a crotchet one, a quaver half a beat and a semiquaver a quarter of one. A dot placed after a note adds **half** of that note again — a dotted minim is two beats plus one, so three. The crotchet is the beat here because Grade 1 counts in crotchets; in other time signatures a different note takes the beat, which is why the values are described as ratios rather than as seconds.

teach.smartTip: Read a time signature downwards, never as a fraction: top says how many, bottom says which note. 3/4 is three crotchets, not three quarters of anything.
teach.didYouKnow: ‘Semibreve’ means ‘half-short’ — it was one of the shorter notes in use centuries ago, before faster values arrived.

theoryInSound.prompt: Play the rhythm and tap each strong beat you hear — the beat that feels accented.

lessons.title: Reading notes on the bass stave

objectives: The notes on the bass lines — G, B, D, F, A
The notes in the bass spaces — A, C, E, G
How the bass clef fixes F on the fourth line
The notes just outside the stave — F below it, B above it, and middle C on its ledger line

concept.title: Reading the bass stave
concept.body: The bass clef is the F clef: its two dots sit either side of the fourth line up, which fixes that line as F. The five **lines**, bottom to top, spell G, B, D, F, A — Good Boys Deserve Football Always. The four **spaces** spell A, C, E, G — All Cows Eat Grass. The letters climb through the alphabet exactly as they do in the treble, so the method is the same: find a landmark and count. The lines and spaces sit **lower** than the treble ones, which is the point of a second clef — it saves writing ledger lines for every low note. Notes also sit just outside the five lines. F hangs in the space below the bottom line, and B sits in the space above the top line. Above B comes middle C on a short ledger line, and D in the space above that. Middle C is the note the two staves share: it is one ledger line above the bass and one below the treble.

teach.smartTip: The bass clef is the F clef — its two dots hug the F line, top and bottom.
teach.didYouKnow: Middle C sits just above the bass stave and just below the treble — one note shared between the two clefs.

objectives: Every note value has a matching rest — a silence that lasts exactly as long as the note
A rest fills time in a bar just like a note, so a bar's notes and rests together add up to the full bar
A whole silent bar is written as a semibreve rest, whatever the time signature

concept.title: Silence has a length too
concept.body: A rest is a measured silence, and every note value has a matching rest of the same length: a semibreve rest, a minim rest, a crotchet rest, a quaver rest and a semiquaver rest. Silence is counted, not skipped — the bar still has to add up. To find the rest that completes a bar, do it in three steps. Add up the beats already written. Take that away from the number of beats the time signature asks for. Then choose the rest worth exactly the beats left over.

teach.smartTip: Count the beats already used, take that from the bar, and the rest you need is the silence of whatever is left.
teach.didYouKnow: The semibreve rest hangs down from a line, the minim rest sits on top of one — a tiny difference worth a second look, since they are easy to mix up.

objectives: What a sharp, a flat and a natural each do
That a sharp raises and a flat lowers a note by a semitone
How an accidental lasts to the end of its bar

concept.title: Sharps, flats and naturals
concept.body: An accidental changes a note by a semitone, the smallest step in Western music. A sharp raises the note by a semitone, a flat lowers it by a semitone, and a natural cancels either one and returns the note to its plain letter. The sign is always written **before** the note it changes, even though you say it after — you write the sharp then the F, but you call it F sharp. An accidental lasts for the rest of the bar and applies only to that line or space; the next bar-line clears it. The one exception is a note tied across that bar-line, which keeps the accidental for as long as the tie holds it.

teach.smartTip: An accidental only lasts to the next bar-line — the bar-line wipes the slate clean.
teach.didYouKnow: On a keyboard a sharp and the flat above it can be the same key — C♯ and D♭ are one black note.

objectives: A tie joins two notes into one sound, and their values add
A dot adds half the value again to the note or rest it follows
Work out both in beats, counted against the time signature

concept.title: Two ways to make a note longer
concept.body: Not every length has a note of its own, so there are two ways to write a longer one. A tie is a curved line joining two notes of the **same** pitch. You play the first and hold through the second, so a minim tied to a crotchet is one sound lasting three beats. Do not confuse it with a slur, which curves between **different** pitches and means play them smoothly. A dot does a similar job in less space: a dot after a note or a rest adds half of that value again. A dotted minim is two beats plus one, which is three; a dotted crotchet is one beat plus half, which is one and a half. The dot always takes its half from the note it sits beside, so a dotted quaver is worth three semiquavers, not three of anything else. Rests are dotted exactly the same way.

teach.smartTip: A dot adds half, never double. Halve the note it follows, then add that on.
teach.didYouKnow: The tie exists because a bar line cannot be crossed by a single note. A sound that runs from one bar into the next has to be written as two notes tied together.

objectives: The major scale is built from tones and semitones in a fixed order
Semitones fall between the 3rd and 4th notes, and between the 7th and 8th
Every major key uses the same pattern, which is why they all sound alike

concept.title: Tone, tone, semitone
concept.body: A major scale is not just eight notes in a row. It is a fixed pattern of steps, and the pattern is what makes it sound major. A tone is two semitones — on a keyboard, a step with a note in between. A semitone is the smallest step there is, with nothing in between. Going up from the keynote, a major scale steps tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. That puts a semitone between the 3rd and 4th notes and another between the 7th and 8th, and the other five steps are tones. Because the pattern never changes, every major key sounds the same shape from its own keynote. That is also how the key signature gets decided: the sharps or flats are whatever it takes to make the pattern come out right starting from that note.

teach.smartTip: Two semitones, always in the same places: 3 to 4, and 7 to 8. Everything else is a tone.
teach.didYouKnow: The 7th note is called the leading note because the semitone below the keynote pulls the ear upward. Take that semitone away and the scale stops sounding finished.

lessons.title: Grouping notes, and where the bar-lines go

objectives: Beams join notes shorter than a crotchet into one beat
A new beat always starts a new beam
The same notes beamed differently show a different beat
Add the bar-lines to a rhythm that has none, counting beats from the start

concept.title: Beams show the beat
concept.body:
Quavers and shorter notes are joined by a beam instead of being written with separate tails. The beam is not decoration: it tells the reader where each beat begins. In 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 the beat is a crotchet, so two quavers are beamed together and the next pair starts a fresh beam. Six quavers in 3/4 are written as three joined pairs, never as one long run of six, because a reader has to see three beats. Change the beams and you change what the bar looks like it is in, which is why grouping is part of writing music correctly rather than a matter of taste.

That is also how you put the bar-lines IN. Work along the rhythm adding up beats, and the moment you reach a full bar, a bar-line goes there — between two notes, never through one. Then start counting again at one. Because the beams already show the beats, you can often see where a bar ends without counting note by note. The double bar at the very end is printed for you.

teach.smartTip: Beam within a beat, break between beats. Count the beat first, then draw the beams.
teach.didYouKnow: Before beams, everything was written with separate tails. Beaming spread with printed music in the 1500s and made rhythm readable at speed.

objectives: The six volume levels, from pianissimo to fortissimo
That mezzo means "half", so it pulls the word it sits with toward the middle
The words and hairpins that ask for a **gradual** change

concept.title: How loud to play
concept.body: Dynamics are the words that say how loud. Six of them form one scale, quietest to loudest: pianissimo (pp) very quiet, piano (p) quiet, mezzo piano (mp) moderately quiet, mezzo forte (mf) moderately loud, forte (f) loud, fortissimo (ff) very loud. Only two Italian words are really at work there — piano and forte — and mezzo means "half", so it pulls whichever word it sits with back toward the middle. Three more ask for a gradual change rather than a level: crescendo gets gradually louder, while diminuendo and decrescendo both mean gradually quieter.

teach.smartTip: Read the letters, not the words: one p or f is quiet or loud, two is very, and an m in front moves it toward the middle.
teach.didYouKnow: The instrument is named after the dynamics — the "pianoforte" was the first keyboard that could play both soft and loud depending on how hard you pressed.

objectives: The key signatures for C, G, D and F major
That the key signature applies right through the piece
The order sharps and flats are written in

concept.title: Grade 1 key signatures
concept.body: A key signature is the group of sharps or flats printed just after the clef, and it applies to every bar that follows until the music says otherwise — you do not have to keep writing the accidental in. Grade 1 asks for four keys. C major has nothing at all. G major has one sharp, F sharp. D major has two sharps, F sharp and C sharp. F major has one flat, B flat. Count the symbols first, then decide: one sharp is G major, two sharps is D major, one flat is F major, and none is C major.

teach.smartTip: One sharp is G major and one flat is F major — the two quickest to name at a glance.
teach.didYouKnow: Sharps are always written in the same order — F, C, G, D, A, E, B — each a fifth above the last. Grade 1 never needs more than the first two.

objectives: The five speed words in order, from adagio to allegro
The words that change the speed rather than set it
How a metronome mark states a speed as a number

concept.title: How fast to play
concept.body: Tempo is the speed. Five words set it, and they belong in order from slowest to fastest: adagio slow, andante at a walking pace, moderato at a moderate speed, allegretto fairly quick, allegro quick and lively. Three more change a speed already running: accelerando gets gradually faster, while rallentando and ritardando both mean gradually slower. After either of those, a tempo says go back to the original speed. A metronome mark states the speed exactly instead of describing it — a crotchet followed by = 120 means 120 crotchet beats a minute.

teach.smartTip: Andante is a walking pace — if you can walk to it, that is roughly the speed.
teach.didYouKnow: Allegro literally means "cheerful" in Italian rather than "fast" — the speed came from the mood, not the other way round.

objectives: Name any note of a major scale by its degree number
The keynote is the 1st degree, so the count starts at one, not zero
The rule is the same in C, G, D and F

concept.title: Counting from the keynote
concept.body: Every note of a scale has a number. The keynote is the *1st degree*, the note above it the 2nd, and so on up to the 7th. Count letter names, and always start the count on the keynote itself — that is the mistake to avoid, because the keynote is 1, not 0. In C major, C is the 1st degree, D the 2nd, E the 3rd. Change key and the numbers stay put: in G major, G is now the 1st degree and A the 2nd. The number describes a note's **position** in its scale, not its letter, which is why the same note is a different degree in a different key.

teach.smartTip: The keynote is the 1st degree, not the 0th. Count letter names from it, including it.
teach.didYouKnow: Numbering degrees instead of naming notes is what lets a tune be described once and played in any key. A folk musician calling a phrase '1-3-5' has said something true in every key at once.

objectives: How to name an interval by its number
That you count both the lower and upper notes
The intervals from a 2nd up to an octave
At this grade the lower note is always the keynote of the scale

concept.title: Counting intervals
concept.body: An interval is the distance between two notes, and at Grade 1 it is named by a number alone. Count the **letter names** from the lower note to the upper, and count both ends. C up to G is C, D, E, F, G — five letters, so a 5th. The commonest mistake is counting the gaps instead of the notes, which gives an answer one too small. Two names are special: the same note twice is a unison, and eight letters apart, where the letter comes round again, is an octave. Accidentals do not change the number — only the letters count. At Grade 1 the lower note is always the keynote, so every interval you are asked for is measured up from it. Later grades ask for the distance between any two notes.

teach.smartTip: Count the lower note as ‘one’ — intervals include both ends, not just the gaps between.
teach.didYouKnow: An octave spans eight notes because the eighth note repeats the first — the letter names come back around.

objectives: Build the tonic triad of a major key in root position
The tonic triad is the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees stacked
Root position means the keynote is the lowest note

concept.title: Three notes that fix the key
concept.body: A *triad* is three notes stacked in 3rds. The *tonic triad* is the one built on the 1st degree, the keynote. Take the keynote, skip a letter, take the next, skip again, take the next: in C major that is C, E and G — the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees. It is called root position when the keynote is at the bottom. Every major key has one, and it is the chord a piece in that key most often begins and ends on, which is why it sounds settled.

teach.smartTip: Stack the 1st, 3rd and 5th degrees. Skip a letter each time, starting on the keynote.
teach.didYouKnow: The tonic triad is why a piece can 'sound like' its key within a bar. Three notes are enough to point at it strongly, which is what a composer relies on when a piece opens with a chord rather than a tune.

objectives: The marks that change how a note is played — legato, staccato, accent
The difference between a slur and a tie, which look identical
The marks that tell you where to go — repeats, D.C. and Fine

concept.title: The marks on the page
concept.body: Some marks change how a note sounds. Legato means smoothly, and a slur — a curved line over notes of **different** pitch — asks for exactly that. Staccato means short and detached, written as a dot above or below the notehead. An accent is a small wedge asking for extra emphasis. Cantabile means in a singing style and dolce means sweetly. A tie looks exactly like a slur but joins two notes of the **same** pitch, and it makes one longer note rather than two. A pause holds a note longer than written. Repeat marks send you back to the opening repeat sign, or to the very beginning if there is no opening repeat sign; D.C. (da capo) means go back to the beginning, and Fine marks where to stop.

teach.smartTip: Slur or tie? Look at the two noteheads. Same pitch is a tie and you play one note; different pitches is a slur and you play them all, smoothly.
teach.didYouKnow: Fine is Italian for "end" and is said FEE-nay — nothing to do with the English word.

lessons.title: Music in context — reading a passage

objectives: How to read a whole passage bar by bar
How to find the highest and lowest notes in a melody
How to compare note lengths across bars

concept.title: Reading a passage bar by bar
concept.body: A passage is read a bar at a time. Bars are numbered from the first full bar, and questions point at one of them: which bar holds the highest note, the lowest note, or the longest note. Work along the stave and compare the bars against each other rather than trying to judge one on its own. Highest and lowest mean position on the stave, not volume — a quiet note high up is still the highest. Longest means the note held for the most beats, which is a question about note **value**, not about pitch.

teach.smartTip: Highest and lowest mean the position on the stave, not how loud a note is.
teach.didYouKnow: Bar numbers are a fairly modern habit — they spread in the 1800s as scores grew long enough that players needed a way to say where to restart.
